edges.relationship: In Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023), written with Pat Hudson, Berg returns to Eric Williams's thesis in Capitalism and Slavery (1944) that slavery's profits helped finance British industrialisation; Nicholas Radburn's review (2024) reads the book as offering new perspectives on the Williams thesis and helping to substantiate it.
edges.evidence_note: Mediated by Radburn's review in Continuity and Change (2024), read on Cambridge Core: 'offer new perspectives on the Williams thesis'; 'helps to substantiate Williams' thesis'. Pat Hudson's own Williams edge (edge_3966) is unchanged. The book was not read here; the claim is the reviewer's characterisation. Added at the user's request (2026-11-02: 'Berg and Hudson should be connected to Eric Williams and the slavery debate').
edges.map_label: Revisits and substantiates the Williams thesis (2023, with Hudson)

sources.title: Nicholas Radburn, review of M. Berg and P. Hudson, Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (Polity, 2023), Continuity and Change 39:1 (2024): 127–.
sources.citation: Nicholas Radburn, review of Maxine Berg and Pat Hudson, Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (London: Polity, 2023), Continuity and Change 39:1 (May 2024), 127ff.

verification.note: Review text read on the publisher's own Cambridge Core page (2026-11-02). It opens with Williams's 1944 claim that slavery's profits 'provided one of the main streams of that accumulation of capital in England which financed the industrial revolution', says the book 'seeks to synthesize existing scholarship to offer new perspectives on the Williams thesis', and concludes that it 'helps to substantiate Williams' thesis'. The book itself was not read here.

rationale: Berg and Hudson's 2023 book is the major recent restatement of the Williams thesis; the timeline linked Hudson to Williams but not Berg.
